1.plans: Round 1 (exploratory): start at 2.99, a mid-range price that keeps a healthy margin of 1.99 while staying well under the 4.51 ceiling. Record units sold and profit per unit over a fixed observation window. Round 2: test a higher price (about 3.49) and a lower price (about 2.49) to see how volume responds. Round 3: refine around whichever price gives the highest total profit (units x (price - 1.00)), using steps of roughly 0.25 to 0.50. Keep the price below 4.51 at all times, since no customer would pay more. Compare profit, not just volume, when choosing.
1.insights: With no demand data, the profit-maximizing price is unknown, so the choice rests on the structure of the problem. Profit = (p - 1.00) x Q(p). Since Q(p) falls as p rises and the hard ceiling is 4.51, the optimum is likely in the middle of the range, not at either extreme. A price near 1.00 earns almost nothing per unit even with high volume, and a price near 4.51 risks losing most buyers. 2.99 is a sensible opening test because it sits in the lower-middle of the feasible range and is a common price point that buyers tend to accept. Final price decisions should be driven by observed profit data.
